strengths: ECAD offers a useful formulation of diffusion caching as multi-objective search over component-, block-, and timestep-level decisions, producing a selectable quality-efficiency frontier rather than a few fixed operating points.

The empirical study is broad: three DiT architectures, multiple prompt sets, FID/CLIP/ImageReward metrics, several caching baselines, 256×256 and 1024×1024 evaluations, and both model- and resolution-transfer experiments.

Results are consistently strong. Several schedules improve both measured quality and acceleration over prior caching approaches, including substantial FID gains, and the learned frontiers provide finer operating-point control.

The paper includes useful ablations on population size, calibration-set size, samples per prompt, and calibration-set choice, along with detailed schedule visualizations and reasonably clear genetic-algorithm specifications.
The method is training-free with respect to model parameters and can incorporate prior schedules, making it practically complementary to existing caching techniques.
weaknesses: The schedule-search cost is a major unquantified limitation. For PixArt-α alone, the stated setup entails roughly 550×72×1,000 = 39.6 million calibration image generations. GPU-hours, energy, wall-clock time, storage requirements, and the number of downstream inferences needed to amortize this cost are not reported. This substantially weakens the claims of scalability and easy off-the-shelf deployment.

The evaluation does not include human preference judgments. Because ImageReward is the optimization objective, unexpectedly large automatic-metric improvements over the unaccelerated model may reflect metric-specific selection or exploitation. FID is not a prompt-alignment measure, and nearly unchanged CLIP scores do not fully validate claims of sharper images or improved adherence.

There are no repeated evolutionary runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Performance may depend on population initialization, fixed seeds, and stochastic genetic operations; reporting a single frontier after hundreds of generations leaves robustness unclear.

Latency comparisons are imperfect. PixArt latency is reported as per-image throughput from batches of 100 rather than true single-request latency, while ToCa and DuCa values are normalized from separate implementations whose unaccelerated runtimes differ by roughly 5–6×. This makes the headline latency comparisons less conclusive for real deployment.

The novelty is moderate: the central algorithm is largely a direct application of NSGA-II and standard crossover/mutation to a binary caching mask. The main contribution is therefore empirical search engineering rather than a new optimization or caching principle.

The paper sometimes overstates what is established. A genetic search returns an empirical nondominated set, not a guaranteed Pareto-optimal or 'best-case' frontier; likewise, adaptation is not entirely seamless because cacheable components must be manually identified and instrumented for each architecture.

The selection rule for the named 'fast,' 'faster,' and 'fastest' schedules is not fully specified, creating concern that evaluation-set metrics could have influenced operating-point selection. Exact machine-readable schedules and the promised code link are also absent from the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.

Evaluation is restricted to 20-step image generation and one GPU family. Results across samplers, step counts, hardware, single-image inference, and newer architectures would be needed to establish the claimed generality.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and offers a flexible component-, block-, and timestep-level representation of diffusion caching schedules.
The empirical study covers three diffusion-transformer models, several datasets and metrics, two resolutions, and both model- and resolution-transfer settings.
Several reported operating points improve the speed-quality trade-off over FORA, TGATE, ToCa, and DuCa, particularly for PixArt-alpha at 256x256.
The appendix describes the evolutionary operators, initialization heuristics, cacheable components, and latency setup in useful detail.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: ECAD is essentially NSGA-II applied to a binary caching mask. There is no comparison against random search, greedy search, or other optimization strategies, so the gains cannot be attributed to the genetic algorithm rather than the large search budget and strong heuristic initialization.

The calibration cost is enormous and insufficiently discussed. The stated PixArt-alpha search alone evaluates roughly 550 x 72 x 1,000 = 39.6 million generated images; FLUX adds about 6 million. The paper reports neither total GPU-hours nor monetary or energy cost, and provides no amortization analysis showing when inference savings recover this expense. This substantially weakens the practicality, scalability, and environmental claims.

The evaluation lacks repeated search runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Selecting schedules after evaluating millions of samples creates substantial selection effects, making run-to-run variability and robustness particularly important.

Quality is evaluated almost entirely with automatic metrics, including the same learned reward used for optimization. FID and CLIP provide some out-of-domain evidence, but no human evaluation validates the claimed preservation or improvement of perceptual quality; the qualitative comparisons are sparse and appear selectively chosen.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. Several relevant recent caching and acceleration methods are cited but not evaluated, while the main comparisons focus on a small set of methods. There is also no controlled comparison using an equal search or tuning budget.

The latency methodology conflates latency with batched throughput: PixArt measurements use batches of 100 and divide batch time by batch size. Moreover, ToCa and DuCa times are normalized across substantially different implementations whose unaccelerated runtimes differ by more than fivefold. This does not establish fair single-image or deployment latency.

Claims of discovering a Pareto-optimal or best-case frontier are too strong: the method only finds an empirical nondominated set within a tiny sampled portion of a combinatorial space, with no optimality guarantee. The manuscript also claims to avoid human-defined hyperparameters despite using multiple genetic hyperparameters and carefully designed initialization heuristics.

Some conclusions overstate the tables. At 1024x1024, the transferred ECAD schedule is worse than ToCa on several PartiPrompts and MJHQ metrics and improves COCO FID only slightly. Formal presentation is also inconsistent about whether the quality objective is minimized or maximized, and the cited reference for NSGA-II appears to be an NSGA-III paper.

Reproducibility is limited in the supplied manuscript: the code URL is blank, selected schedules are primarily shown as heatmaps rather than machine-readable masks, and reproducing the search would require a prohibitive, undocumented compute budget.

strengths: ECAD offers a useful, training-free formulation of diffusion caching as multi-objective schedule search, producing many fine-grained quality–latency operating points instead of a few manually designed configurations.
The empirical study is broad: three diffusion-transformer models, multiple prompt and image benchmarks, several quality metrics, measured latency and MACs, and both 256×256 and 1024×1024 generation.

The reported results are consistently competitive. For example, on PixArt-α the fastest ECAD schedule reaches a 2.58× speedup while substantially improving COCO FID over the similarly accelerated ToCa and DuCa configurations; strong results are also reported for FLUX-1.dev.

The transfer experiments are valuable: schedules transfer across PixArt variants and from 256×256 calibration to 1024×1024 FLUX inference with limited degradation, supporting the claimed adaptability.

The algorithm and schedule representation are clearly explained, and the appendix provides useful implementation details, search-budget ablations, latency methodology, and visualizations of discovered schedules.
weaknesses: The offline search cost is extremely large and insufficiently reported or contextualized. The main PixArt-α run nominally evaluates 550×72 schedules with 1,000 generated images per schedule—roughly 39.6 million generations. Wall-clock time, total GPU-hours, energy use, and the number of deployments required to amortize this cost are missing, weakening the practicality and scalability claims.

There is no equal-budget comparison against random search, local or greedy search, Bayesian optimization, or another generic schedule optimizer. Consequently, the experiments demonstrate that extensive black-box search finds good schedules, but do not isolate whether the genetic algorithm is important.

The paper calls the discovered schedules Pareto-optimal and even “best-case,” although they are only non-dominated among evaluated candidates; no optimality guarantee or search-coverage analysis is provided.

Quality evidence relies entirely on automatic metrics, including the Image Reward metric used for optimization. Cross-metric FID and CLIP evaluations help, but a human preference study and confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are absent, leaving uncertainty about perceptual gains and metric overfitting.

Latency is reported as per-image throughput at the largest fitting batch size with precomputed text embeddings, which may not represent interactive batch-one latency. ToCa and DuCa latencies are additionally normalized across separate implementations rather than measured in one unified stack, limiting the precision of speed comparisons.

The baseline set omits empirical comparisons to several cited recent automatic or dynamic caching approaches. Reproducibility would also benefit from machine-readable release of all reported schedules and complete accounting of the search procedure and compute budget.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant formulation of diffusion caching as multi-objective schedule optimization, producing a selectable speed-quality Pareto frontier rather than a few manually tuned operating points.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: three diffusion-transformer models, several established caching baselines, multiple prompt datasets, measured latency and MACs, and complementary quality metrics including FID, CLIP, ImageReward, GenEval, and DPG-Bench.

The reported results are compelling. ECAD frequently improves both latency and quality over prior caching methods, including strong FLUX.1-dev acceleration and notable FID improvements on unseen COCO and MJHQ prompts.
Resolution, model, and inference-step transfer experiments provide useful evidence that the learned schedules are not entirely tied to the exact calibration configuration.

The appendix contains valuable ablations of reward choice, calibration prompts, population initialization, search budget, and genetic-algorithm hyperparameters. The method and experimental setup are generally explained clearly.
weaknesses: The main algorithmic novelty is limited: ECAD primarily applies standard NSGA-II to a binary caching mask. There is no comparison against equally budgeted random search, greedy/local search, Bayesian optimization, or another black-box optimizer, so the evidence does not establish that the genetic algorithm itself is necessary or particularly effective.

Schedule discovery is extremely expensive: the principal PixArt frontier costs roughly 700 A6000 GPU-hours, while the method evaluates tens of millions of generated images. Costs for all reported model searches, especially FLUX.1-dev, are not fully quantified. This weakens claims of scalability and practical accessibility even if the cost can eventually be amortized.

Results are reported from apparently single optimization and evaluation runs without confidence intervals, repeated-search variance, or statistical tests. This is important because evolutionary search, generated images, ImageReward, and finite-sample FID are all stochastic, and many candidate schedules are considered.

The search directly optimizes ImageReward on fixed prompts and seeds, yet no human-preference evaluation is provided. Generalization to unseen automatic metrics and datasets is encouraging, but it does not rule out reward-model exploitation or establish perceptual equivalence to uncached generation.

Some claims are overstated. NSGA-II only finds an empirical non-dominated set and does not justify terms such as “best-case” or “Pareto-optimal” over the enormous schedule space. Likewise, caching intermediate activations necessarily requires some persistent storage, making the repeated “no memory overhead” claim insufficiently substantiated by measurements.

Latency comparisons partly normalize speedups across different codebases rather than measuring every method within one unified implementation. Together with precomputed text embeddings, unusually large batch sizes, and only a few measured batches, this limits conclusions about absolute latency and deployment scenarios such as batch-one inference.

ECAD remains specialized per architecture, sampler, and step count; the transfer experiments show degradation and often require additional search. The paper does not evaluate video generation or other modalities despite suggesting that the framework naturally extends to them.

Reproduction of the headline results is burdensome because of the search cost, and the paper does not expose uncertainty across hardware, seeds, or independent evolutionary runs. Exact machine-readable schedules and complete end-to-end cost accounting would materially improve reproducibility.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant formulation of diffusion caching as multi-objective optimization over generation quality and computational cost.

The empirical study is broad: three diffusion-transformer models, several datasets and quality metrics, multiple speed-quality operating points, and transfer across model variants, resolutions, and inference-step counts.
ECAD often reports substantially better automatic-metric trade-offs than the evaluated caching baselines, including on prompt sets not used during schedule search.
The appendix provides useful implementation details and ablations covering population initialization, calibration prompts, reward choice, evolutionary hyperparameters, and optimization cost.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: ECAD is essentially NSGA-II applied to a binary component-caching mask, using standard crossover and mutation. The paper does not establish a deeper algorithmic contribution beyond applying expensive black-box search to this domain.

The search cost is extremely high—approximately 700 A6000 GPU-hours and tens of millions of generated calibration images for the full PixArt frontier. Describing the method as requiring only a small calibration set obscures the very large number of repeated evaluations, and weakens the claimed scalability and accessibility.

Baseline fairness is questionable. ECAD receives a massive per-model optimization budget, whereas competing methods use fixed or transferred hyperparameters; ToCa is explicitly evaluated on PixArt-Σ with settings that the authors acknowledge are suboptimal. This does not cleanly show that evolutionary optimization is superior to comparably budgeted tuning of competing approaches.

There is no human evaluation despite optimizing directly against Image Reward and making strong claims about preserved or improved perceptual quality. CLIP, FID, Image Reward, GenEval, and DPG-Bench do not rule out reward exploitation or perceptually undesirable changes, particularly after selecting among tens of thousands of schedules.

The reported latency is predominantly per-image throughput obtained from very large batches—up to batch size 100—rather than interactive batch-one latency. Competitor timings are additionally normalized across separate implementations instead of being measured in one controlled codebase, limiting the reliability of the practical speed claims.

The paper provides no uncertainty estimates, repeated evolutionary runs, or statistical significance analysis. Consequently, it is unclear how stable the discovered frontiers and sometimes modest metric differences are with respect to search randomness and image-generation seeds.

The repeated claim that ECAD introduces “no memory overhead” appears technically unsupported: retaining component outputs across denoising steps necessarily requires cache storage relative to ordinary uncached inference. The paper does not quantify ECAD's own peak-memory overhead.

Claims that the framework naturally extends to video, other modalities, quantized models, and arbitrary human-defined objectives are speculative; experiments cover only text-to-image DiTs. Overall, the extensive results are promising, but the limited novelty, costly and asymmetrical comparison, and insufficient validation of perceptual quality leave the paper marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/49c8ab7d951e419785f1e36c4af52eba/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a clear and practically useful formulation of component-level diffusion caching as multi-objective optimization, producing selectable quality-latency Pareto frontiers rather than isolated operating points.

The empirical results are compelling: across PixArt-alpha, PixArt-Sigma, and FLUX.1-dev, ECAD generally improves the speed-quality trade-off over established caching baselines. Particularly strong evidence includes 2.58x FLUX acceleration without degrading GenEval and approximately 2x PixArt acceleration with improved FID.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering three architectures, two resolutions, several prompt distributions, FID, CLIP, ImageReward, GenEval, DPG-Bench, measured latency, and computational cost. Results on unseen prompts reduce concern that schedules merely overfit the calibration reward.

The paper includes useful transfer experiments across model variants, resolutions, and inference-step counts, alongside extensive ablations of prompt selection, population size, reward choice, genetic hyperparameters, and initialization.

The method is training-free, requires no model-weight modification, adds no inference-time memory overhead, and yields reusable schedules, making its inference gains practically relevant despite the offline search cost.

The presentation is clear and technically detailed; the binary schedule representation, evolutionary operations, latency protocol, component costs, and limitations are documented sufficiently well to support implementation.
weaknesses: The central algorithmic novelty is moderate: applying NSGA-II with crossover and bit-flip mutation to a binary caching mask is conceptually straightforward. The main contribution is therefore empirical and formulation-based rather than a substantial new optimization technique.

The paper does not compare NSGA-II against equal-budget random search, local search, Bayesian optimization, or another black-box optimizer. The initialization ablation is not a substitute for this comparison, so it remains unclear how much of the gain comes from the genetic algorithm rather than extensive evaluation of many schedules seeded by strong heuristics.

Search cost is substantial—up to roughly 700 A6000 GPU-hours for the reported PixArt frontier and 470 hours for the highlighted SOTA schedule. The cheaper 44-hour result is encouraging but weaker, and this cost limits the claim that ECAD seamlessly adapts to arbitrary off-the-shelf models.

No repeated search runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests are reported. Because genetic search, image generation, and metric estimation are stochastic—and some improvements over the uncached model are surprising—run-to-run stability is insufficiently established.

Some latency comparisons are normalized using each baseline implementation's relative speedup instead of measuring all methods within one common optimized implementation. The very different raw baseline runtimes make the resulting absolute-latency comparisons less conclusive.

There is no human-preference study, although ImageReward is the search objective and several headline claims concern perceptual quality. FID, CLIP, GenEval, and DPG-Bench provide valuable corroboration but do not fully exclude reward-specific artifacts.

Claims such as discovering a “best-case” or “Pareto-optimal” frontier are too strong: ECAD finds an empirical nondominated set within its explored schedules, without establishing global Pareto optimality. Generalization claims beyond image generation are also speculative, as video and other modalities are not evaluated.
